text: I’ll model the water as the union of the centred spherical cavity and six radial cylindrical passages clipped by the 40 mm cube, then subtract the free 15 mm ball. This interpretation makes each “hole” a short face-to-cavity passage (not a full 40 mm bore). I’ll use the exact CAD faces for patch extraction, then generate a coarse body-fitted tetrahedral mesh with Gmsh. First I’m building and inspecting the fluid solid in metres.

The Boolean is a single connected water solid with 21 boundary faces: 8 spherical remnants of the hollow wall, 6 cylindrical hole-wall faces, 6 planar openings, and 1 spherical ball face. I’ll now render the coarse CAD boundary and inspect each cylindrical face’s exact axis so patch assignment is based on its generating surface rather than bounding-box location.

The preview confirms the intended six-lobed exterior and the internal ball boundary. The two x-directed cylindrical faces share the same unsigned CAD axis, so I’ll distinguish their signs using the face centroid only after confirming the axis; the other four are directly identified likewise. Next I’ll export the 14 requested patch STLs from the exact classified faces and print independent radius checks from the planar opening areas and full ball area.

All 14 patch files now exist before meshing. The ball radius and all six opening radii measure exactly 15 mm and 12 mm from their CAD areas. I’ll transfer the same exact water solid to Gmsh via STEP and inspect Gmsh’s retained surface types/centres before assigning physical patch IDs.

Gmsh preserves the same 21-face topology, so patch tagging can be reproduced unambiguously by surface type and signed centre of mass. For the coarse mesh I’ll use 0.8 mm tetrahedral sizing—small enough to represent the 1 mm clearance while keeping this first mesh modest—and name the 14 surface groups plus the water volume.

The coarse mesh contains about 194k tetrahedra and 40k points; Gmsh reports no ill-shaped tetrahedra after optimization. I’ll now convert it to OpenFOAM and inspect the converted boundary table before running the binding mesh check.

Conversion retained exactly the 14 requested boundary names; the converter’s temporary “undefined faces” message refers to boundary faces before it maps the physical surface elements, and no `defaultFaces` patch remains afterward. I’ll run full `checkMesh -allGeometry -allTopology` now.

The mesh itself was not read because this OpenFOAM build requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries even for the extended check. I’ll add minimal valid dictionaries and rerun the same check; this changes no mesh or boundary condition.
The extended checker also parses the standard scheme subdictionaries. I’ll supply empty/default-only scheme sections (still no fields or boundary conditions) and retry.

The exhaustive optional diagnostics find 571 boundary tetrahedra with only two internal faces (a known algebraic determinant warning for pure tetrahedral boundary cells) and 2 low interpolation-weight faces; all standard geometric metrics pass, including 68.5° max non-orthogonality and 0.925 max skewness. Since completion is bound to the standard `checkMesh`, I’ll run that exact check now and retain the exhaustive log as disclosed diagnostics.

Standard `checkMesh` reports **Mesh OK**: one region, 193,795 tetrahedra, 14 patches, closed boundary, and valid volume. Before declaring completion, I’ll verify that the 14 independently exported STL patches weld into one closed union and list their triangle counts; this catches patch-edge tessellation mismatches that the volume mesh cannot reveal.

The independently tessellated CAD patch files leave 48 unmatched edge segments at patch junctions, despite representing the correct surfaces. I won’t waive that: I’ll replace them with patch STLs extracted from the conformal Gmsh boundary triangulation, preserving the same CAD-derived patch assignments while guaranteeing shared edge nodes.

The replacement STLs now use exactly the same boundary triangles as the OpenFOAM mesh. I’ll recheck welded closure and explicitly count same-direction shared edges to validate winding consistency before completion.

The conformal STL union is now fully closed and consistently wound: 37,108 triangles, zero free edges, zero non-manifold edges, and zero same-direction edge pairs. One final geometric check will sample the underlying spherical faces to confirm the hollow radius and the 1 mm minimum ball clearance directly from the CAD surfaces.
